summary:
Erzincan province stands under the Turkish national legal framework. No Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident or court decision was found on record, so what a trans visitor faces in the province is determined by national law and national policing practice.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions or same-sex adoption, and with a bar on LGBTI people serving openly in the military.

Since 2015 the Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia. In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

Freedom-of-assembly exposure extends to ordinary LGBT advocacy: ILGA-Europe reported on 7 December 2020 that 19 human rights defenders were prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, and urged Turkish courts to acquit them and dismiss all charges. Even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution in Turkey, and a visitor in Erzincan would be judged under that same framework.
tangentialFactors:
The national climate of Pride bans and prosecutions, documented in Ankara and Istanbul, sets the tone for how visible LGBT advocacy is treated across Turkey's provinces, including Erzincan. A trans visitor who attends or is perceived to attend a public LGBT gathering in the province would fall under the same assembly and public-order regime.

Turkey's low standing in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking, 47th of 49, reflects a national pattern of weak legal protection rather than any Erzincan-specific measure.
localsOnly:
Erzincan residents live under the national framework: same-sex relationships, marriage and civil unions carry no legal recognition, and LGBTI people cannot serve openly in the military. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in law, though the practical value of that protection is contested.

Local Pride or LGBT visibility events, if organised, would be subject to the same ban-and-dispersal pattern documented elsewhere in Turkey since 2015, and participants could face prosecution as occurred at the 2019 Ankara campus march.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Erzincan-specific enforcement data, police practice records or court decisions were located in the source inventory; the province-level picture rests on the absence of such records rather than on documented local practice.

Whether the early-2026 reported proposal to criminalise public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality" has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.
